history.heading: Phosphate island
paragraphs: Christmas Island, in the Indian Ocean about 350 km south of Java, was named by a British captain who passed it on Christmas Day 1643. It was uninhabited until the late 19th century.

Britain annexed it in 1888 after phosphate deposits were found, and workers from China, Malaya and elsewhere were brought to mine them. Japan occupied the island during the Second World War. Sovereignty was transferred from Singapore to Australia in 1958.

culture.heading: A multicultural community
paragraphs: The small population is mostly of Chinese and Malay descent, with Australians of European origin. English is official, and Chinese and Malay are widely spoken. Buddhist temples, mosques and churches stand side by side, and Chinese New Year and Hari Raya are celebrated.
The island is famous for the annual migration of tens of millions of red crabs from the forest to the sea to breed, which covers roads and beaches.

politics.heading: Australian external territory
paragraphs: Christmas Island is an external territory of Australia, administered by an administrator appointed by the Australian government, with a local shire council. Residents vote in Australian federal elections. Australia has operated an immigration detention centre on the island.

economy.heading: Mining and nature
paragraphs: Phosphate mining has been the main industry for over a century. Most of the island is a national park, and nature tourism, diving and birdwatching are growing. Government services also provide jobs. The currency is the Australian dollar.
